claim_1.claim: ELISA analysis of serum from healthy human donors showed no significant correlations between EBV seropositivity and the immune biomarkers measured in this study compared to EBV-seronegative individuals.

sources.quote: We also analyzed EBV-infected (EBV+) versus uninfected (EBV−) individuals, but the classification model was unable to distinguish EBV+ from EBV − subjects (the accuracy for the logistic regression model is lower that 50%) and multiple regression analysis (adjusted for age and sex) showed that the most significant EBV-related immune feature is only detected at a False Discovery Rate (FDR) of 75% (Q = 0.75) (Fig. S3a), suggesting no significant correlations with the immune biomarkers measured in this study.

claim_2.claim: Transcription profiling by array analysis of whole blood from young CMV-infected versus young CMV-uninfected adults showed up-regulation of immune activation genes, including elevated module 103, module 30, and modules including several KIR2 and KIR3 genes as well as GZMH, compared to young CMV-uninfected adults.

sources.quote: At the gene expression level, the CMV effect independent of age was an up-regulation of genes associated with immune activation.

For example, expression of module 103 (antigen processing and presentation, P < 0.00001 and NK cell mediated cytotoxicity, P < 0.00001) was elevated in yCMV+ (Fig. 1) and this module includes several KIR2 and KIR3 genes as well as GZMH
The expression of the gene module 30 was also elevated in yCMV+ (Fig. 1)

claim_3.claim: Transcription profiling by array analysis of whole blood from older CMV-uninfected versus young CMV-uninfected adults showed down-regulation of gene modules associated with cell cycle, protein synthesis, amino-acid metabolism, cell-death, ubiquitination pathway, HIF1α signaling, LXR/RXR activation, and carbohydrate metabolism in older adults compared to young adults.

sources.quote: The age effect independent of CMV (yCMV− vs oCMV−) revealed down-regulation of several gene modules (Fig. 1) including those associated with cell cycle (module 34 and 101, P = 0.019), protein synthesis (module 35 and 39, P = 0.0009 and P < 0.0001, respectively) amino-acid metabolism (module 43, P = 0.0023), cell-death (modules 47 and 54, P = 0.0021 and P < 0.0001, respectively), the ubiquitination pathway (module 98, P = 0.0092), HIF1α signaling (module 101, P < 0.0001), LXR/RXR activation, which is involved in cholesterol and lipid metabolism (module 102, P = 0.007) and the metabolism of carbohydrates (module 108, P = 0.00074).

claim_4.claim: Flow Cytometry analysis of PBMCs from young CMV-infected versus young CMV-uninfected adults showed higher CD8+ pSTAT1 and pSTAT3 responses to IL-6 in CMV-infected individuals compared to CMV-uninfected individuals.

sources.quote: In particular, we found an elevation of circulating IL-13 and IFN-γ cytokines, and higher CD8+ pSTAT1 and pSTAT3 responses to IL-6 in CMV+ individuals in the younger cohort compared to the CMV− subjects (Fig. 1).

claim_5.claim: Flow Cytometry analysis of PBMCs from young CMV-infected versus older CMV-infected adults showed that older CMV-infected individuals were defective in the IL-6-responsive CD8+ pSTAT1/pSTAT3 pathway compared to young CMV-infected individuals.

sources.quote: It is interesting to note that compared to yCMV+ subjects, the oCMV+ individuals are defective in this pathway (Table S2, yCMV+ vs oCMV+), which suggests a degree of adaptation to chronic levels of inflammatory cytokines in older CMV-infected subjects.

claim_6.claim: Flow Cytometry analysis of PBMCs from CMV-infected versus CMV-uninfected human donors showed that the frequency of CD4+ CD28− cells was higher in CMV-infected individuals, and this frequency was not significantly affected by age.

sources.quote: We restricted our analyses to SNPs with minor allele frequency greater than 5% (116,405 SNPs) (see Methods) and focused on the frequency of CD4+ CD28− cells, a hallmark of CMV infection (48) and the level of which is not significantly affected by age.

claim_7.claim: Luminex xMAP analysis of serum from young CMV-infected versus young CMV-uninfected adults showed elevated circulating IL-13 and IFN-γ in CMV-infected individuals compared to CMV-uninfected individuals.

sources.quote: In particular, we found an elevation of circulating IL-13 and IFN-γ cytokines, and higher CD8+ pSTAT1 and pSTAT3 responses to IL-6 in CMV+ individuals in the younger cohort compared to the CMV− subjects (Fig. 1).

claim_8.claim: Hemagglutination Inhibition analysis of serum from vaccinated young and older adults at day 0 and 28±7 days after influenza vaccination (day 28±7) showed a negative effect of age on antibody response, and higher antibody responses in young CMV-infected than young CMV-uninfected subjects, while CMV-related differences were not significant in the older cohort.

sources.quote: To probe the immune system’s response in a standardized manner, we used seasonal trivalent inactivated influenza vaccination (IIV) and assayed antibody responses using the standard hemagglutinin-inhibition (HAI) assay at day 0 and 28±7 days after vaccination (Fig. S1)
As expected, a negative effect of age was observed in the antibody response to IIV (P < 0.0001) (Fig. 2a).
Surprisingly, in the yCMV+ group the antibody response was higher than in yCMV− subjects (P = 0.03) (Fig. 2a). These CMV-related differences were not significant in the older cohort (Fig. 2a and b).

claim_9.claim: Hemagglutination Inhibition analysis of serum from 77 individuals who returned one year later during the 2009-2010 influenza season showed a positive effect of CMV in the young but not the older cohort compared to CMV-uninfected individuals.

sources.quote: A similar positive effect of CMV in the young (P = 0.04) but not the older cohort was observed in the 77 individuals who returned one year later during the 2009-2010 influenza season (Fig. 2b).

claim_10.claim: Hemagglutination Inhibition analysis of serum from an independent cohort of 37 young individuals recruited during the 2010-2011 influenza season showed validated higher influenza vaccine responses in CMV-infected compared to CMV-uninfected individuals.

sources.quote: In addition, these findings were validated in an independent cohort of 37 young individuals recruited during the 2010-2011 influenza season (P = 0.017) (Fig. 2c).

claim_11.claim: Single-nucleotide polymorphism assay analysis of genomic DNA from CMV+ human subjects showed 35 SNPs associated with the frequency of CD4+ CD28− cells at FDR lower than 5%.

sources.quote: We identified 35 SNPs (on chromosomes 6, 9, 12, 14, 15, 17 and 19) associated with the frequency of CD4+ CD28− cells, at a false discovery rate (FDR) lower than 5% (P < 5 × 10−6, FDR Q < 0.05) (Fig. S4).

claim_12.claim: plaque assay analysis of infected mouse lung tissue from influenza A-challenged mice showed reduced influenza viral titers at day 7 after influenza A virus challenge in MCMV-infected mice with early latency (>5 weeks after MCMV infection, day >35) and established latency (12 weeks after MCMV infection, day 84) compared to mock-infected mice, but this difference was lost after long-standing latency (9 months after MCMV infection, about day 270).

sources.quote: Mice were considered in early latency at >5 weeks, established latency at 12 weeks, and long-standing latency at 9 months after MCMV infection.

Both in early and established latency, we observed better protection against influenza in the MCMV-infected (IAV+ MCMV+) versus the mock-infected (IAV+ MCMV−) mice at day 7 after IAV challenge as seen by the reduced influenza viral titers in the lungs (Fig. 3a and b). In contrast, in older mice exposed to long-standing MCMV infection these differences were lost (Fig. 3c).

claim_13.claim: Flow Cytometry analysis of BAL cells from influenza A-challenged mice showed higher influenza-specific CD8+ T cell responses against the PA, PB1, and NP epitopes in animals with early latency (>5 weeks after MCMV infection, day >35) and established latency (12 weeks after MCMV infection, day 84), but not after long-standing latency (9 months after MCMV infection, about day 270), compared to mock-infected mice.

sources.quote: Mice were considered in early latency at >5 weeks, established latency at 12 weeks, and long-standing latency at 9 months after MCMV infection.

Consistent with this observation, the influenza-specific CD8+ T cell responses against the three major influenza epitopes (DbPA224--233 (PA), KbPB1703-711 (PB1), and DbNP366-374 (NP)) in BAL cells were higher in animals with early and established latency, but not after long-standing latency compared with the mock-infected group (Fig. 3d-f).

claim_14.claim: plaque assay analysis of infected mouse lung tissue from IFN-γ knockout versus control mice challenged with influenza A at 5 weeks after MCMV infection (day 35) showed significantly higher viral titers in IFN-γ knockout mice compared to control mice.
